transcript.content: Hello. I'm glad you're here today. What brings you in to see me?

I'm seeking help because I've been struggling with severe mood swings, going from deep depression to periods of extreme, uncontrollable energy. Along with that, I've been hearing and seeing things that other people don't. This has all been going on for over two years now.
Do you ever hear or see these things during times when your mood feels completely normal and stable, or do they only happen when you are feeling very high or very low?

Yes, I definitely do. There was a period of about two or three weeks where my mood felt completely normal and stable, but I was still hearing and seeing those things. It wasn't tied to feeling really high or really low at all during that time.
Over the past two years, would you say that these mood swings—the highs and the lows—have been present for the majority of the time you've been unwell?

Yes, absolutely. For most of the past two years, I've been dealing with those intense mood swings, especially the times when my energy is through the roof. It feels like those high and low periods have taken up the vast majority of the time I've been struggling.

latest_inference.note: Previously, the candidates were Schizoaffective Disorder (Bipolar Type) and Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features. The patient confirmed experiencing auditory and visual hallucinations during a 2-to-3-week period of stable, normal mood, and that mood symptoms have been present for the majority of the overall illness. This fulfills the DSM-5 criteria for Schizoaffective Disorder (Bipolar Type) and rules out Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features, where psychosis occurs exclusively during mood episodes.

This presentation strongly suggests a bipolar spectrum disorder or a schizoaffective disorder. The initial differentials are Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features, Schizoaffective Disorder (Bipolar Type), Bipolar I Disorder, and Bipolar II Disorder. Further exploration is needed to determine the relationship between the psychotic symptoms and the mood episodes.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient exhibits both major mood episodes (manic and depressive) and psychotic symptoms (hallucinations) over a two-year period. Crucially, the psychotic symptoms occurred for a period of 2-3 weeks in the absence of any prominent mood symptoms, meeting the DSM-5 criteria for Schizoaffective Disorder. The presence of manic episodes (periods of extreme, uncontrollable energy) specifies the Bipolar Type.
